claim: Rhythmic neural circuits generate spatiotemporal patterns of activity by synaptic interactions between neuronal populations.
source: Rhythmic neural circuits, which are ubiquitous in nervous systems (Buzsáki, 2006), generate spatiotemporal patterns of activity by synaptic interactions between neuronal populations
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Buzsáki, 2006, which provides established knowledge about rhythmic neural circuits.

claim: The method presented can extract and separate patterns of inhibitory and excitatory synaptic conductances at high temporal resolution from single neuronal intracellular recordings in rhythmically active networks.
source: Here, we present a general method for extracting and separating patterns of inhibitory and excitatory synaptic conductances at high temporal resolution from single neuronal intracellular recordings in rhythmically active networks.
evidence: This is a primary claim about the method developed in this study, supported by the experimental data and analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The post-synaptic conductances reflect the combined synaptic inputs from the key interacting neuronal populations and can reveal the functional connectome of the active circuits.
source: These post-synaptic conductances reflect the combined synaptic inputs from the key interacting neuronal populations and can reveal the functional connectome of the active circuits.
evidence: This claim is based on the inference from the experimental data and the theoretical framework presented in the study.

claim: The method is applicable to any periodically active network where the oscillation period greatly exceeds the interspike intervals and membrane time constant of individual neurons.
source: The technique is applicable to any periodically active network where the oscillation period greatly exceeds the interspike intervals and membrane time constant of individual neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on the theoretical principles underlying the method and is supported by inference from the mathematical framework.

claim: The approach extends previously proposed methods by providing nearly continuous, high-resolution readouts of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic conductances.
source: Our approach extends previously proposed methods for extracting dynamic patterns of input synaptic conductances from intracellular recordings from neurons in a variety of circuits (Borg-Graham et al., 1998; Anderson et al., 2000; Shu et al., 2003; Berg et al., 2007; Endo and Kiehn, 2008; Wright Jr and Calabrese, 2011) by providing nearly continuous, high-resolution readouts of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic conductances that are essential for deciphering circuit functional interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous methods and by the data presented showing higher temporal resolution.

claim: The mammalian brainstem respiratory CPG is a fundamental rhythmic neural system that generates and controls breathing movements critical for homeostatic regulation of oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH.
source: To illustrate the utility of our technique, we applied this to circuits in the mammalian brainstem respiratory CPG, which is the fundamental rhythmic neural system that generates and controls breathing movements that are critical for homeostatic regulation of oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH in the brain and body (Feldman and Smith, 1995; Richter and Smith, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on the respiratory CPG.

claim: The rhythmic patterns of alternating inspiratory and expiratory phase neuronal activities originate within interacting pontine-medullary excitatory and inhibitory circuits in the brainstem.
source: The rhythmic patterns of alternating inspiratory and expiratory phase neuronal activities that coordinate activity of spinal and cranial motoneurons during breathing originate within interacting pontine-medullary excitatory and inhibitory circuits in the brainstem (Cohen, 1979; Bianchi et al., 1995; Feldman and Smith, 1995; Richter, 1996; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature on respiratory circuits.

claim: The respiratory cycle period in the in situ rat brainstem-spinal cord preparation typically spans approximately 3–4 s.
source: The respiratory cycle period in our in situ rat brainstem-spinal cord preparation typically spans approximately 3–4 s (Figures 1 and 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The time resolution of the method is roughly 1/300 of the respiratory cycle period.
source: The respiratory cycle period in our in situ rat brainstem-spinal cord preparation typically spans approximately 3–4 s (Figures 1 and 2), yielding a time resolution of roughly 1/300 of the period.
evidence: This claim is based on a calculation from the membrane time constant and cycle period data.

claim: The phase-specific current-voltage dependencies are almost perfectly linear in a wide range of voltage values.
source: This figure illustrates that the phase-specific current-voltage dependencies are almost perfectly linear in a wide range of voltage values.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hyperpolarizing current injection protocol drives the membrane potential to values between –100 and –60 mV to minimize voltage-dependent currents.
source: To ensure that voltage-dependent currents are minimized during the recording, a hyperpolarizing current injection protocol is employed. This involves injecting a negative current into the neuron, which drives the membrane potential to a more negative value. In our test recordings, the membrane potential was typically held between –100 and –60 mV, and we primarily analyzed the data for these hyperpolarized voltages.
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the experimental protocol described.

claim: At hyperpolarized membrane potentials (–100 to –60 mV), most voltage-gated ion channels are closed and do not significantly contribute to neuronal current-voltage relationships.
source: At this hyperpolarized state, most voltage-gated ion channels are closed and do not significantly contribute to the neuronal current-voltage (I-V) relationships and affect interpretations of our conductance analyses.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of ion channel biophysics and is supported by the linear I-V relationships observed in the data.

claim: The respiratory cycle consists of three main activity phases: inspiratory (I), post-inspiratory (post-I), and stage 2 or late expiratory (E2).
source: Under normal physiological conditions, the neuronal activity during the respiratory cycle consists of three main activity phases [inspiratory (I), post-inspiratory (post-I), and stage 2 or late expiratory (E2)] that are well documented in the literature (e.g. Lindsey et al., 2012; Richter and Smith, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on respiratory physiology.

claim: Pre-I/I cells receive decrementing expiratory inhibition and augmenting excitation during late expiration, as well as strong ramping inspiratory excitation.
source: Pre-I/I cells (n=25 neurons recorded in the preBötC) in all cases received decrementing expiratory inhibition and augmenting excitation during late expiration, as well as strong ramping inspiratory excitation (Figures 3A1—5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 25 neurons shown in Figure 3.

claim: Two out of 13 labeled pre-I/I neurons were identified as inhibitory neurons (1 glycinergic and 1 GABAergic).
source: We labeled 13 of these pre-I/I neurons during recording, two of which were identified as inhibitory neurons by neurotransmitter immuno-labeling for glycine or GABA (1 glycinergic and 1 GABAergic neuron identified)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data from labeled neurons.

claim: Ramp-I neurons receive ramping inspiratory phase excitation and strong synaptic inhibition throughout the post-inspiratory and late-expiratory (E2) phases.
source: Neurons with the ramp-I spiking patterns (n=24 recorded in preBötC) also received ramping inspiratory phase excitation, but unlike some pre-I/I cells, they generally showed strong synaptic inhibition throughout the post-inspiratory and late-expiratory (E2) phases (Figures 3B1—5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 24 neurons shown in Figure 3.

claim: Four out of seven labeled ramp-I neurons were identified as inhibitory (glycinergic) neurons.
source: Four out of seven of these neurons were labeled in the preBötC and identified as inhibitory (glycinergic) neurons
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data from labeled neurons.

claim: All early-I spiking neurons showed decrementing expiratory phase inhibition.
source: All early-I spiking neurons (n=6 in preBötC) showed decrementing expiratory phase inhibition (Figures 3C1—5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 6 neurons shown in Figure 3.

claim: One of three labeled early-I neurons was identified as an inhibitory (GABAergic) neuron.
source: One of the three labeled early-I neurons was identified as an inhibitory (GABAergic) neuron (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Late-I cells receive inhibitory inputs from post-I and aug-E neurons and excitation from pre-I/I and ramp-I neurons, plus concurrent inspiratory phase inhibition.
source: Synaptic inputs to late-I cells (n=6 in preBötC) were similar to ramp-I neurons (Figures 3D1—5) plus concurrent, inspiratory phase inhibition. So, in addition to inhibitory inputs from post-I and aug-E neurons and pre-I/I (in some cases) and ramp-I excitation, they likely receive inhibitory inputs from early-I spiking neurons (Figure 4D1).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data from 6 neurons shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Post-I spiking neurons received strong decrementing inhibition during inspiration and incrementing inhibition during late expiration.
source: Post-I spiking neurons (n=40: 25 in preBötC, 15 in BötC) that always exhibit a decrementing firing pattern during expiration received strong decrementing inhibition during inspiration and incrementing inhibition during late expiration (Figures 3E1—5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 40 neurons shown in Figure 3.

claim: Eight of 20 labeled post-I neurons were identified as glycinergic.
source: Eight of the 20 post-I neurons labeled (five in preBötC and three BötC neurons) were identified as glycinergic (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), consistent with a previous study (Ezure et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data and is consistent with a cited previous study.

claim: All aug-E spiking neurons received decrementing inhibitory inputs during expiratory and inspiratory phases, as well as an excitatory input that started in the middle of expiration and incremented towards the end of expiration.
source: Finally, all the aug-E spiking neurons (n=19 recorded: nine neurons in preBötC, 10 in BötC) received decrementing inhibitory inputs during expiratory and inspiratory phases, as well as an excitatory input that started in the middle of expiration and incremented towards the end of expiration (Figures 3F1—5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 19 neurons shown in Figure 3.

claim: Three out of six labeled aug-E neurons were identified as glycinergic neurons (one preBötC neuron and two BötC neurons).
source: Three out of six of these neurons labeled were identified as glycinergic neurons (one preBötC neuron and two BötC neurons) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The shapes of the conductance profiles and the relationship between excitatory and inhibitory conductances extracted from current-clamp and voltage-clamp recordings are very similar.
source: Figure 5 shows the excitatory and inhibitory synaptic conductance profiles extracted from current- (left) and voltage-clamp (right) segments of the intracellular recordings for three different types of representative neurons. It is evident that the shapes of the conductance profiles, as well as the relationship between the excitatory and inhibitory conductances, extracted are very similar.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data shown in Figure 5.

claim: While absolute conductance values vary with reversal potentials, the shapes of synaptic profiles and the relationship between excitatory and inhibitory conductances remain consistent across different values of reversal potentials.
source: Figure 6 illustrates that although the absolute values of the conductances vary to some extent as we vary the reversal potentials, the shape of their reconstructed profiles remains consistent.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6 testing different reversal potential values.

claim: Differences between results for different recording epochs were comparable to those observed in recordings obtained by current- and voltage-clamp protocols from the same neuron.
source: We found that differences between the results for different epochs in most cases were comparable to those observed in the recordings obtained by current- and voltage-clamp protocols from the same neuron.
evidence: This claim is based on comparative analysis of data from different recording epochs.

claim: The inhibitory synaptic reversal potentials retrieved varied significantly among cells between –62 mV and –116 mV.
source: Interestingly, the inhibitory synaptic reversal potentials retrieved turned out to vary significantly among cells between –62 mv and –116 mV.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental measurements from multiple neurons.

claim: The length constant of the neuron and the distance of the microelectrode from the synaptic inputs determine the measured reversal potential in intracellular recordings.
source: It is well known that in intracellular recordings, the length constant of the neuron and the distance of the microelectrode from the synaptic inputs determine the measured reversal potential (Calvin, 1969; Spruston et al., 1993; Wehr and Zador, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on intracellular recording techniques.

claim: The estimate of the timing of synaptic conductances is reliable and not influenced by the length constant of the neuron.
source: Importantly, Wehr and Zador, 2003 show that the estimate of the timing of synaptic conductances is reliable and not influenced by the length constant of the neuron.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wehr and Zador, 2003.

claim: Phasic excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs that result from network interactions shape membrane potential trajectories and spiking patterns of respiratory neurons throughout the respiratory cycle.
source: Indeed, our results suggest that phasic excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs that result from network interactions of these respiratory neuron populations shape membrane potential trajectories and spiking patterns of the neurons throughout the respiratory cycle.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on synaptic conductances.

claim: The synaptic conductance profiles are consistent with multiple features of the network architecture and interactions proposed by Smith et al., 2007.
source: Our synaptic conductance profiles are consistent with multiple features of the network architecture and interactions proposed by Smith et al., 2007 as illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the current data with a previously published model.

claim: The method is based on the general mathematical framework involving current balance equations and linear regression to separate excitatory and inhibitory conductances.
source: The method is based on the general mathematical framework presented, involving current balance equations and linear regression to separate excitatory and inhibitory conductances, and therefore is applicable to different rhythmic neuron types and circuits and is suitable for diverse experimental setups.
evidence: This claim describes the theoretical foundation of the method.

claim: The technique ensures high-resolution temporal profiling of synaptic inputs, making it adaptable to a wide range of rhythmically active neuronal circuits.
source: Our technique ensures high-resolution temporal profiling of synaptic inputs, making it adaptable to a wide range of rhythmically active neuronal circuits such as vertebrate and invertebrate motor pattern generation (CPG) networks (e.g., Calabrese and Marder, 2025), and cortical circuit rhythms (Yuste et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by the theoretical framework and citations to other rhythmic circuits.

claim: The approach is compatible with various experimental setups, including current-clamp and voltage-clamp protocols.
source: We designed our method to be compatible with various experimental setups, including current-clamp and voltage-clamp protocols, by focusing on the fundamental principles of electrophysiology and network dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental validation using both recording protocols.

claim: The coefficient of variation of the respiratory cycle period was <10% for analyzed recordings.
source: We only analyzed recordings from respiratory neurons that fulfilled the following criteria: (1) The coefficient of variation of the respiratory cycle period was <10%
evidence: This is a methodological criterion used for data selection.

claim: At least three steps of current injections were made during intracellular recording that were kept constant for at least 5 respiratory cycles each for analyzed recordings.
source: At least three steps of current injections were made during intracellular recording that were kept constant for at least 5 respiratory cycles each.
evidence: This is a methodological criterion used for data selection.

claim: The preBötC region contains local excitatory and inhibitory circuit neurons critical for generating rhythmic inspiratory activity.
source: For our illustration of extracting synaptic conductances with the above approach, we targeted neurons in key interacting respiratory circuits located in discrete bilateral regions of the ventrolateral medulla, specifically in the preBötzinger complex (preBötC) region, which contains local excitatory and inhibitory circuit neurons critical for generating rhythmic inspiratory activity
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the preBötC region.

claim: The BötC region contains neurons generating rhythmic expiratory activity that interact with preBötC circuits, including by inhibitory circuit connections.
source: and the adjacent more rostral Bötzinger complex (BötC) region (refer to Figure 2—figure supplement 1), containing neurons generating rhythmic expiratory activity that interact with preBötC circuits, including by inhibitory circuit connections (e.g. Lindsey et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2013; Molkov et al., 2017; Ausborn et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on the BötC region.

claim: All animal procedures were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (Animal Study Proposal #1154–21).
source: All animal procedures were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (Animal Study Proposal #1154–21).
evidence: This is a statement of ethical approval for the study.

claim: Experiments were performed using in situ arterially perfused brainstem-spinal cord preparations from mature (3–4-wk-old) rats.
source: Experiments were performed using the in situ arterially perfused brainstem-spinal cord preparations from mature (3–4-wk-old) rats (Paton, 1996; Paton et al., 2022)
evidence: This describes the experimental preparation used in the study.

claim: A hydraulic damping Windkessel chamber was used in the perfusion circuit to eliminate peristaltic flow pulsations that affect the stability of sharp electrode intracellular recordings.
source: A hydraulic damping Windkessel chamber was used in the perfusion circuit immediately downstream from the output of the roller pump (Watson-Marlow, Wilmington, MA) to eliminate peristaltic flow pulsations that affect the stability of the sharp electrode intracellular recordings.
evidence: This describes a methodological detail to improve recording stability.

claim: The total conductance has static (phase-independent) and dynamic (phase-dependent) components.
source: The total conductance has static (phase-independent) and dynamic (phase-dependent) components. The latter is assumed to be a sum of dynamic components of the inhibitory and excitatory synaptic conductances.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on the mathematical framework of the method.

claim: The linear upper boundary of the trajectory in wedge diagrams was seen in almost all recordings processed, implying that during certain phase(s) of the respiratory cycle, the interneurons receive only inhibitory input.
source: Interestingly, the linear upper boundary of the trajectory was seen in almost all recordings processed, implying that, first, during certain phase(s) of the respiratory cycle, the interneurons indeed receive only inhibitory input
evidence: This claim is based on observation of data patterns across multiple recordings.

claim: The profiles of neuronal synaptic interactions are specific for the in situ reduced rat brainstem-spinal cord system and cannot account for supra-brainstem and peripheral circuit inputs in vivo.
source: We note that the profiles of neuronal synaptic interactions that we consider are specific for the in situ reduced rat brainstem-spinal cord system, which has proven to be an important model system for understanding the operation of core CPG respiratory circuits in the medulla and pontine reticular formation that are operational in our experimental set-up (Paton et al., 2022), but cannot account for the supra-brainstem and peripheral circuit inputs in the nervous system in vivo (e.g. Lindsey et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2013; Paton et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim acknowledges the limitations of the experimental preparation used.
